articles.title: Backpacking Diplomacy: Israeli Backpackers in Himachal Pradesh, India
Passover in a Pandemic: Public Religious Discourse and Lay Relationships to Rabbinic Authority
articles.abstract: Abstract Though scholars of Orthodox Judaism have long been interested in shifting patterns of religious authority, relatively little empirical work has been done on how lay people relate to halachic authority in their ordinary lives. This article draws from an interview study of halachically observant Jews who straddle the Orthodox–non-Orthodox boundary. It takes as a case study a novel halachic decision people had to make early in the coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic, namely, whether to use videoconferencing during the Passover seders. Global rabbinic conversations on the topic were public and easily accessible to lay people, who used them for halachic guidance in lieu of community rabbis. At the same time, the local community remained relevant as practitioners engaged in social modeling to decide what to do. Use of the public rabbinic discourse reflects two analytically distinct ways of engaging with halachic authority; one way takes halachic arguments as expert guides to understanding halachic principles, that is, as epistemic authority. The other way relies on rabbinic rulings as inherently valid by virtue of the authority of the rabbinic office. The article adds to research suggesting that liberal observant lay people regularly make halachic judgments for themselves, but also shows that the authority of rabbis remains relevant in this community.
